meta.topic: 线性代数：初等矩阵、秩、分块矩阵、矩阵幂与多项式、QR/SVD、广义逆、矩阵群

zh: 设 $A=(a_{ij})$ 为 $m\times n$ 矩阵。对 $E_m$ 做一次初等行变换得到 $m$ 阶**初等矩阵** $P$；由于 $P$ 的第 $i$ 行就是行变换后单位阵的第 $i$ 行，$PA$ 的第 $i$ 行等于 $A$ 各行按该行系数的线性组合。三种情形分别是：交换第 $i,j$ 行时 $(PA)_{i*}=A_{j*}$、$(PA)_{j*}=A_{i*}$；第 $i$ 行乘 $k\ne0$ 时 $(PA)_{i*}=kA_{i*}$；把第 $j$ 行的 $k$ 倍加到第 $i$ 行时 $(PA)_{i*}=A_{i*}+kA_{j*}$。同理，对 $E_n$ 做列变换得到 $n$ 阶初等矩阵 $Q$，则 $AQ$ 对 $A$ 做同样的列变换。结论：**左乘初等矩阵实现相应的行变换，右乘实现相应的列变换**；左乘因子必须是 $m$ 阶，右乘因子必须是 $n$ 阶。

三类初等矩阵的行列式可直接按定义计算：交换型 $|E(i,j)|=-1$；倍乘型 $|E(i(k))|=k$（要求 $k\ne0$）；倍加型 $|E(i,j(k))|=1$。三者都非零，所以初等矩阵都可逆。逆矩阵仍是同类型的初等矩阵：交换两次回到原状，故 $E(i,j)^{-1}=E(i,j)$；倍乘的逆是 $E(i(1/k))$；倍加的逆把 $k$ 换成 $-k$，即 $E(i,j(k))^{-1}=E(i,j(-k))$。验证只需注意对应的行变换互相抵消，例如先加 $k$ 倍再加 $-k$ 倍就回到 $E$。

若 $A$ 可逆，高斯消元把 $A$ 化为行最简形；可逆矩阵的行最简形必为 $E$，否则会出现零行、秩小于 $n$，与可逆矛盾。每步行变换对应左乘一个初等矩阵，因此存在初等矩阵 $E_1,\dots,E_k$ 使 $E_k\cdots E_1A=E$，从而
$$A=E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1},$$
即 $A$ 是有限个初等矩阵的乘积。反过来，初等矩阵可逆，其乘积也可逆。对增广矩阵 $[A\mid E]$ 做同样的行变换，相当于左乘 $P=E_k\cdots E_1$：
$$P[A\mid E]=[PA\mid P]=[E\mid A^{-1}],$$
所以右半就是 $A^{-1}$。这里只能做行变换；混入列变换会破坏左右两半的对应关系，结果不再是 $A^{-1}$。

设 $P$ 可逆。$PA$ 的每一行是 $A$ 的行的线性组合，故 $\operatorname{row}(PA)\subseteq\operatorname{row}(A)$；又 $A=P^{-1}(PA)$，反向包含也成立，所以 $\operatorname{row}(PA)=\operatorname{row}(A)$。取 $P$ 为初等矩阵，即得初等行变换保持行空间，从而保持行秩。类似地，右乘可逆矩阵 $Q$ 保持列空间：$\operatorname{col}(AQ)=\operatorname{col}(A)$，故初等列变换保持列空间与列秩。由于行秩等于列秩（见矩阵的秩），初等行变换和列变换都不改变秩。注意方向：行变换一般会改变列空间，列变换一般会改变行空间，不能反过来说。

设 $r=r(A)$。先用行变换把 $A$ 化为行最简形，此时主元列为 $r$ 个标准基向量；再用列变换把主元列依次换到前 $r$ 列，并用它们消去其余列中的非零元，得到
$$PAQ=\begin{pmatrix}E_r&O\\O&O\end{pmatrix},$$
其中 $P,Q$ 都是初等矩阵的乘积，因而可逆。于是同型矩阵 $A,B$ 可经有限次初等变换互化，当且仅当 $r(A)=r(B)$。这个矩阵称为 $A$ 的**等价标准形**；注意它不是相似标准形：这里 $P,Q$ 一般不相同，也不要求 $Q=P^{-1}$。

例：$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$。构造 $[A\mid E]$ 并只做行变换：$$\begin{aligned}&\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\3&4&0&1\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad\xrightarrow{r_2-3r_1}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\0&-2&-3&1\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad\xrightarrow{-\frac12r_2}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\0&1&\frac32&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad\xrightarrow{r_1-2r_2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-2&1\\0&1&\frac32&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}$$ 于是 $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\\frac32&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}$。验证：$AA^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$。整个过程每一步都是左乘初等矩阵，正对应“左乘 = 行变换”；若把某一步换成列变换，右半就不再是 $A^{-1}$。
en: Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $m\times n$ matrix. Applying one elementary row operation to $E_m$ produces an $m\times m$ **elementary matrix** $P$. The $i$-th row of $P$ records the coefficients of the operation, so the $i$-th row of $PA$ is the corresponding linear combination of the rows of $A$. The three cases are: swapping rows $i,j$ gives $(PA)_{i*}=A_{j*}$ and $(PA)_{j*}=A_{i*}$; multiplying row $i$ by $k\ne0$ gives $(PA)_{i*}=kA_{i*}$; adding $k$ times row $j$ to row $i$ gives $(PA)_{i*}=A_{i*}+kA_{j*}$. Similarly, applying a column operation to $E_n$ yields an $n\times n$ elementary matrix $Q$, and $AQ$ performs that column operation on $A$. Conclusion: **left multiplication by an elementary matrix performs the corresponding row operation, while right multiplication performs the corresponding column operation**; the left factor must be $m\times m$ and the right factor $n\times n$.

The determinants of the three types follow directly from the definition: a swap has $|E(i,j)|=-1$; a scaling has $|E(i(k))|=k$ with $k\ne0$; a shear has $|E(i,j(k))|=1$. All are nonzero, so every elementary matrix is invertible. The inverse is again elementary of the same type: a swap is self-inverse, $E(i,j)^{-1}=E(i,j)$; a scaling inverts its factor, $E(i(k))^{-1}=E(i(1/k))$; a shear changes $k$ to $-k$, $E(i,j(k))^{-1}=E(i,j(-k))$. Indeed the corresponding row operations cancel: adding $k$ times a row and then $-k$ times it restores $E$.

If $A$ is invertible, Gaussian elimination reduces it to reduced row echelon form, which must be $E$; otherwise a zero row would appear, the rank would be less than $n$, and $A$ could not be invertible. Each row operation is left multiplication by an elementary matrix, so there are elementary matrices $E_1,\dots,E_k$ with $E_k\cdots E_1A=E$, hence
$$A=E_1^{-1}\cdots E_k^{-1},$$
a finite product of elementary matrices. Conversely, elementary matrices are invertible and so is any product of them. Applying the same row operations to the augmented matrix $[A\mid E]$ means left multiplication by $P=E_k\cdots E_1$:
$$P[A\mid E]=[PA\mid P]=[E\mid A^{-1}],$$
so the right half is $A^{-1}$. Only row operations are allowed here; mixing in column operations destroys the correspondence between the two halves and the result is no longer $A^{-1}$.

Let $P$ be invertible. Every row of $PA$ is a linear combination of the rows of $A$, so $\operatorname{row}(PA)\subseteq\operatorname{row}(A)$; since $A=P^{-1}(PA)$, the reverse inclusion also holds and $\operatorname{row}(PA)=\operatorname{row}(A)$. Taking $P$ elementary shows that elementary row operations preserve the row space, hence the row rank. Similarly, right multiplication by an invertible $Q$ preserves the column space, $\operatorname{col}(AQ)=\operatorname{col}(A)$, so elementary column operations preserve the column space and the column rank. Because row rank equals column rank (see the rank node), both types of elementary operations preserve the rank. The direction matters: row operations usually change the column space, and column operations usually change the row space; the converse statements are false.

Let $r=r(A)$. Use row operations to reach reduced row echelon form, whose pivot columns are $r$ standard basis vectors; then use column operations to move the pivot columns to the first $r$ positions and to clear the remaining entries in the non-pivot columns. This yields
$$PAQ=\begin{pmatrix}E_r&O\\O&O\end{pmatrix},$$
where $P$ and $Q$ are products of elementary matrices, hence invertible. Therefore two matrices of the same size are interconvertible by finitely many elementary operations exactly when $r(A)=r(B)$. This is the **equivalence normal form** of $A$. It is not a similarity normal form: $P$ and $Q$ are generally different and need not satisfy $Q=P^{-1}$.

Example: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$. Form $[A\mid E]$ and use row operations only: $$\begin{aligned}&\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\3&4&0&1\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad\xrightarrow{r_2-3r_1}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\0&-2&-3&1\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad\xrightarrow{-\frac12r_2}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1&0\\0&1&\frac32&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}\\&\quad\xrightarrow{r_1-2r_2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-2&1\\0&1&\frac32&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}$$ Hence $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\\frac32&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}$. Check: $AA^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Every step is left multiplication by an elementary matrix, exactly matching “left multiplication = row operation”; replacing any step by a column operation would make the right half fail to be $A^{-1}$.

zh:
在 $m\times n$ 矩阵 $A$ 中任取 $k$ 行与 $k$ 列，交点处的 $k^2$ 个元素按原次序组成的 $k$ 阶行列式，称为 $A$ 的一个 $k$ 阶**子式**。若存在非零的 $r$ 阶子式，而所有 $r+1$ 阶子式（只要存在）全为零，就称 $r$ 为 $A$ 的**秩**，记作 $r(A)$；零矩阵规定 $r(O)=0$。由于 $k$ 阶子式要求 $k\le m$ 且 $k\le n$，总有
$$0\le r(A)\le\min\{m,n\}.$$
这个定义不依赖消元过程，但需要检查大量子式；下面给出等价的、可操作的刻画。

用初等行变换把 $A$ 化为行阶梯形 $R$，设 $R$ 有 $r$ 个非零行。行变换保持行空间，而 $R$ 的 $r$ 个非零行线性无关（主元位置逐行右移），所以行秩等于 $r$。行变换不改变列向量之间的线性关系：若 $P$ 可逆，则 $\sum c_j(PA)_{\cdot j}=0\iff P\sum c_jA_{\cdot j}=0\iff\sum c_jA_{\cdot j}=0$，故列秩也等于 $R$ 的列秩；而 $R$ 的 $r$ 个主元列线性无关，非主元列都是它们的线性组合，所以列秩也是 $r$。于是
$$\text{行秩}=\text{列秩}=r.$$
最后，$R$ 中取 $r$ 个主元行与主元列得到非零的 $r$ 阶子式，而任意 $r+1$ 阶子式所在子矩阵至多有 $r$ 个非零行，故其行列式为 $0$。初等变换对应左乘或右乘可逆矩阵，由 Cauchy–Binet 公式，非零子式的最高阶数不变，所以这个 $r$ 也等于定义中的秩。

设 $A$ 为 $m\times n$、$B$ 为 $n\times p$。$AB$ 的第 $j$ 列是 $A$ 的第 $j$ 个列组合：
$$(AB)_{\cdot j}=A(B_{\cdot j}),$$
所以 $\operatorname{col}(AB)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A)$，取维数得 $r(AB)\le r(A)$。另一方面，若 $Bx=0$，则 $ABx=0$，故 $\ker B\subseteq\ker(AB)$；由秩–零化度定理，
$$r(AB)=p-\dim\ker(AB)\le p-\dim\ker B=r(B).$$
两式合并即得
$$r(AB)\le\min\{r(A),r(B)\}.$$
当 $A$ 可逆时 $r(AB)=r(B)$，当 $B$ 可逆时 $r(AB)=r(A)$，因为可逆矩阵乘法不改变秩；但一般情形只能保证这个上界。

对和的情形，$(A+B)x=Ax+Bx$ 表明
$$\operatorname{col}(A+B)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A)+\operatorname{col}(B),$$
于是
$$r(A+B)\le\dim(\operatorname{col}A+\operatorname{col}B)\le r(A)+r(B).$$
这个不等式一般不能取等号：取 $A=E_2$、$B=-E_2$，则 $A+B=O$，左边为 $0$，右边为 $2+2=4$。它只给出上界，不能由 $r(A+B)$ 反推 $r(A)$ 或 $r(B)$，也不能把“秩可加”当成普遍规律。

线性方程组 $Ax=b$ 有解，当且仅当 $b$ 属于 $A$ 的列空间，即 $\operatorname{col}(A)=\operatorname{col}(A\mid b)$，这又等价于
$$r(A)=r(A\mid b).$$
若 $A$ 为 $m\times n$、$r(A)=r$ 且方程组有解，取一个特解 $x_0$，则全部解为 $x_0+\ker A$，其维数为 $n-r$。因此：$r=n$ 时零空间为 $\{0\}$，解唯一；$r<n$ 时若解存在则有无穷多解。特别地，$n$ 阶方阵满足
$$A\ \text{可逆}\iff r(A)=n\iff |A|\ne0.$$
这些等价只对方阵成立；矩形矩阵没有“可逆”一说。
en:
Choose any $k$ rows and $k$ columns of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$; the $k\times k$ determinant formed by the $k^2$ entries at their intersections, in the original order, is a **$k$-th order minor** of $A$. If some $r$-th order minor is nonzero while every $(r+1)$-st order minor (whenever it exists) is zero, then $r$ is the **rank** of $A$, written $r(A)$; the zero matrix has rank $0$. Since a $k$-th order minor requires $k\le m$ and $k\le n$,
$$0\le r(A)\le\min\{m,n\}.$$
This definition does not depend on elimination, but it requires checking many minors; the next step gives an equivalent, computable characterization.

Use elementary row operations to reduce $A$ to a row echelon form $R$ with $r$ nonzero rows. Row operations preserve the row space, and the $r$ nonzero rows of $R$ are linearly independent (their pivots move strictly to the right), so the row rank is $r$. Row operations also preserve all linear relations among columns: for invertible $P$, $\sum c_j(PA)_{\cdot j}=0\iff P\sum c_jA_{\cdot j}=0\iff\sum c_jA_{\cdot j}=0$. Hence the column rank of $A$ equals that of $R$. In $R$ the $r$ pivot columns are linearly independent and every non-pivot column is a linear combination of them, so the column rank is also $r$. Therefore
$$\text{row rank}=\text{column rank}=r.$$
Moreover, the $r$ pivot rows and pivot columns of $R$ give a nonzero $r$-th order minor, while any $(r+1)$-st order submatrix has at most $r$ nonzero rows, so its determinant is $0$. Elementary operations amount to multiplication by invertible matrices, and by the Cauchy–Binet formula the largest order of a nonzero minor is unchanged; hence this $r$ is exactly the rank in the definition.

Let $A$ be $m\times n$ and $B$ be $n\times p$. The $j$-th column of $AB$ is a linear combination of the columns of $A$:
$$(AB)_{\cdot j}=A(B_{\cdot j}),$$
so $\operatorname{col}(AB)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A)$ and $r(AB)\le r(A)$. On the other hand, $Bx=0$ implies $ABx=0$, so $\ker B\subseteq\ker(AB)$. By the rank–nullity theorem,
$$r(AB)=p-\dim\ker(AB)\le p-\dim\ker B=r(B).$$
Combining the two bounds,
$$r(AB)\le\min\{r(A),r(B)\}.$$
If $A$ is invertible then $r(AB)=r(B)$, and if $B$ is invertible then $r(AB)=r(A)$, because invertible multiplication preserves rank; in general only the upper bound is guaranteed.

For a sum, $(A+B)x=Ax+Bx$ shows that
$$\operatorname{col}(A+B)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A)+\operatorname{col}(B),$$
hence
$$r(A+B)\le\dim(\operatorname{col}A+\operatorname{col}B)\le r(A)+r(B).$$
Equality can fail: take $A=E_2$ and $B=-E_2$; then $A+B=O$, the left side is $0$, and the right side is $2+2=4$. The inequality gives only an upper bound. One cannot recover $r(A)$ or $r(B)$ from $r(A+B)$, and rank is not additive in general.

The system $Ax=b$ is solvable exactly when $b$ lies in the column space of $A$, that is, $\operatorname{col}(A)=\operatorname{col}(A\mid b)$, which is equivalent to
$$r(A)=r(A\mid b).$$
Suppose $A$ is $m\times n$ with $r(A)=r$ and the system is consistent. Fix one particular solution $x_0$; then the full solution set is $x_0+\ker A$, of dimension $n-r$. Thus if $r=n$ the null space is $\{0\}$ and the solution is unique; if $r<n$ and a solution exists, there are infinitely many. In particular, for an $n\times n$ matrix,
$$A\ \text{invertible}\iff r(A)=n\iff |A|\ne0.$$
These equivalences hold only for square matrices; rectangular matrices are never called invertible.

zh:
设 $A$ 为 $m\times n$，把它的行分成 $m_1,\dots,m_t$ 段、列按 $n=n_1+\cdots+n_s$ 分成 $s$ 段；设 $B$ 为 $n\times p$，把它的行按同样的 $n_1,\dots,n_s$ 分成 $s$ 段、列分成 $p_1,\dots,p_u$ 段。则 $AB$ 可按 $m_i\times p_j$ 分块，并且
$$(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}A_{ik}B_{kj}.$$
理由：$A_{ik}$ 是 $m_i\times n_k$ 块，$B_{kj}$ 是 $n_k\times p_j$ 块，乘积有意义且阶为 $m_i\times p_j$；按元素展开时，求和指标落在第 $k$ 段的项恰好全部收集在 $A_{ik}B_{kj}$ 中。条件可概括为：**左矩阵的列分法与右矩阵的行分法一致**，每个中间维数 $n_k$ 同时匹配。分法不一致时，对应块无法相乘，分块乘法不成立。

分块乘法与普通矩阵乘法一样不满足交换律；而且子块本身是矩阵，$A_{ik}B_{kj}$ 与 $B_{kj}A_{ik}$ 甚至可能阶数不同。即使所有块都是同阶方阵，也不能交换顺序。取 $2\times2$ 块（每块为 $2$ 阶方阵）
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}I&I\\O&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}I&O\\I&I\end{pmatrix},$$
则
$$AB=\begin{pmatrix}2I&I\\I&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad BA=\begin{pmatrix}I&I\\I&2I\end{pmatrix},$$
两者不相等。错误做法是把子块当数字随意交换；正确做法是保持 $A_{ik}B_{kj}$ 的顺序，并逐项检查阶数是否匹配。

分块转置要做两件事：交换子块的位置，并把每个子块自身转置：
$$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}^{\mathrm T}
=\begin{pmatrix}A^{\mathrm T}&C^{\mathrm T}\\B^{\mathrm T}&D^{\mathrm T}\end{pmatrix}.$$
只交换位置而忘记转置子块是常见错误。对分块对角矩阵
$$D=\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\dots,A_s),$$
行列式满足 $|D|=\prod_{i=1}^{s}|A_i|$，且 $D$ 可逆当且仅当每个 $A_i$ 可逆，此时
$$D^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(A_1^{-1},\dots,A_s^{-1}).$$
这两条由行列式按块展开以及分块乘法直接验证；只要有一个对角块奇异，$|D|=0$，整体不可逆。

设 $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\O&B\end{pmatrix}$，其中 $A$ 为 $p$ 阶、$B$ 为 $q$ 阶。若 $A,B$ 都可逆，则 $M$ 可逆，且
$$M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{-1}&-A^{-1}CB^{-1}\\O&B^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$
验证：分块相乘得
$$MM^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}AA^{-1}&A(-A^{-1}CB^{-1})+CB^{-1}\\O&BB^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}E_p&O\\O&E_q\end{pmatrix},$$
其中右上块为 $-CB^{-1}+CB^{-1}=O$。顺序不能写成 $-B^{-1}CA^{-1}$。行列式方面，当 $B$ 可逆时，左乘行列式为 $1$ 的分块矩阵 $\begin{pmatrix}E_p&-CB^{-1}\\O&E_q\end{pmatrix}$ 可把 $M$ 化为 $\operatorname{diag}(A,B)$，故 $|M|=|A||B|$；对一般 $B$，在 $\mathbb R$ 或 $\mathbb C$ 上可逆矩阵稠密，且两边都是矩阵元素的多项式，恒等式仍成立。

设 $A$ 可逆，$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$，其中 $A$ 为 $p$ 阶、$D$ 为 $q$ 阶。有分块分解
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&O\\C&E_q\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}E_p&A^{-1}B\\O&D-CA^{-1}B\end{pmatrix}.$$
直接乘开：右上块为 $A(A^{-1}B)+O=B$，右下块为 $C A^{-1}B+(D-CA^{-1}B)=D$，其余块也对。两个因子都是分块三角矩阵，行列式分别为 $|A|$ 与 $|D-CA^{-1}B|$，所以
$$|M|=|A|\,\bigl|D-CA^{-1}B\bigr|.$$
矩阵 $S=D-CA^{-1}B$ 称为 $A$ 的 **Schur 补**。在 $A$ 可逆的前提下，$M$ 可逆当且仅当 $S$ 可逆。这个公式要求 $A$ 可逆；若改用 $D$ 可逆的版本，公式应相应变为 $|D|\,|A-BD^{-1}C|$，不能混用。

例：$M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&2\\1&0&3\end{pmatrix}$，取
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},\quad C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad D=3.$$
$|A|=2\ne0$，$A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac12\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$，故
$$A^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12-\frac12\cdot2\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac12\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
S=D-CA^{-1}B=3-\left(-\frac12\right)=\frac72.$$
于是 $|M|=|A|\,|S|=2\cdot\frac72=7$。直接按 $3$ 阶行列式展开：$2(3-0)-1(0-2)+1(0-1)=6+2-1=7$，一致。由于 $S\ne0$，$M$ 可逆；这个例子说明 Schur 补把 $3$ 阶行列式化成了 $1$ 阶行列式。
en:
Let $A$ be $m\times n$, partition its rows into segments of sizes $m_1,\dots,m_t$ and its columns as $n=n_1+\cdots+n_s$. Let $B$ be $n\times p$, partition its rows according to the same $n_1,\dots,n_s$ and its columns into segments of sizes $p_1,\dots,p_u$. Then $AB$ can be partitioned into $m_i\times p_j$ blocks with
$$(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{k=1}^{s}A_{ik}B_{kj}.$$
Reason: $A_{ik}$ is $m_i\times n_k$ and $B_{kj}$ is $n_k\times p_j$, so the product is defined and has size $m_i\times p_j$; in the entrywise expansion, all terms whose summation index lies in the $k$-th segment are collected exactly in $A_{ik}B_{kj}$. The condition is: **the column partition of the left factor must match the row partition of the right factor**, with every intermediate dimension $n_k$ matching. If the partitions do not match, the corresponding blocks cannot be multiplied and block multiplication is invalid.

Block multiplication, like ordinary matrix multiplication, is not commutative; moreover the blocks are themselves matrices, so $A_{ik}B_{kj}$ and $B_{kj}A_{ik}$ may not even have the same size. Even when all blocks are square of the same order, the order cannot be swapped. Take $2\times2$ blocks (each a $2\times2$ matrix)
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}I&I\\O&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}I&O\\I&I\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then
$$AB=\begin{pmatrix}2I&I\\I&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad BA=\begin{pmatrix}I&I\\I&2I\end{pmatrix},$$
which differ. The mistake is to treat blocks as scalars and reorder them freely; the correct procedure keeps the order of $A_{ik}B_{kj}$ and checks the size of every product.

Block transpose requires two operations: transpose the positions of the blocks and transpose each block itself:
$$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}^{\mathrm T}
=\begin{pmatrix}A^{\mathrm T}&C^{\mathrm T}\\B^{\mathrm T}&D^{\mathrm T}\end{pmatrix}.$$
Swapping positions while forgetting to transpose the individual blocks is a common error. For a block diagonal matrix
$$D=\operatorname{diag}(A_1,\dots,A_s),$$
the determinant satisfies $|D|=\prod_{i=1}^{s}|A_i|$, and $D$ is invertible exactly when every $A_i$ is invertible; in that case
$$D^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(A_1^{-1},\dots,A_s^{-1}).$$
Both facts follow directly from Laplace expansion by blocks and block multiplication; if one diagonal block is singular, $|D|=0$ and $D$ cannot be invertible.

Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\O&B\end{pmatrix}$ with $A$ of order $p$ and $B$ of order $q$. If $A$ and $B$ are invertible, then $M$ is invertible and
$$M^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{-1}&-A^{-1}CB^{-1}\\O&B^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$
Verification by block multiplication:
$$MM^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}AA^{-1}&A(-A^{-1}CB^{-1})+CB^{-1}\\O&BB^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}E_p&O\\O&E_q\end{pmatrix},$$
since the upper-right block is $-CB^{-1}+CB^{-1}=O$. The order must not be written as $-B^{-1}CA^{-1}$. For determinants, when $B$ is invertible, left multiplication by the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}E_p&-CB^{-1}\\O&E_q\end{pmatrix}$ (determinant $1$) reduces $M$ to $\operatorname{diag}(A,B)$, so $|M|=|A||B|$. For general $B$, over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ invertible matrices are dense and both sides are polynomials in the entries, so the identity continues to hold.

Let $A$ be invertible and $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}$, with $A$ of order $p$ and $D$ of order $q$. There is a block factorization
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}A&O\\C&E_q\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}E_p&A^{-1}B\\O&D-CA^{-1}B\end{pmatrix}.$$
Multiplying out, the upper-right block is $A(A^{-1}B)+O=B$, the lower-right block is $C A^{-1}B+(D-CA^{-1}B)=D$, and the other blocks match. Both factors are block triangular with determinants $|A|$ and $|D-CA^{-1}B|$, respectively, so
$$|M|=|A|\,\bigl|D-CA^{-1}B\bigr|.$$
The matrix $S=D-CA^{-1}B$ is the **Schur complement** of $A$. Given that $A$ is invertible, $M$ is invertible exactly when $S$ is invertible. This formula requires $A$ invertible; the version using an invertible $D$ reads $|D|\,|A-BD^{-1}C|$ and must not be mixed with it.

Example: $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&2\\1&0&3\end{pmatrix}$ with
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix},\quad C=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad D=3.$$
Since $|A|=2\ne0$, $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12&-\frac12\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, hence
$$A^{-1}B=\begin{pmatrix}\frac12-\frac12\cdot2\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac12\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
S=D-CA^{-1}B=3-\left(-\frac12\right)=\frac72.$$
Therefore $|M|=|A|\,|S|=2\cdot\frac72=7$. Direct expansion of the $3\times3$ determinant gives $2(3-0)-1(0-2)+1(0-1)=6+2-1=7$, in agreement. Since $S\ne0$, $M$ is invertible; the example shows how the Schur complement reduces a $3\times3$ determinant to a $1\times1$ one.

设 $A\in M_n(K)$。定义 $A^1=A$、$A^{k+1}=A^kA$，并约定
$$A^0=E_n.$$
这里 $A^0$ 是单位矩阵，不是数字 $0$ 或 $1$。对固定的 $A$，指数法则
$$A^kA^l=A^{k+l},\qquad (A^k)^l=A^{kl}$$
可对 $l$ 归纳证明：$A^kA^{l+1}=A^kA^lA=A^{k+l}A=A^{k+l+1}$；$(A^k)^{l+1}=(A^k)^lA^k=A^{kl}A^k=A^{k(l+1)}$。证明只用到 $A$ 的各次幂彼此可交换。若 $A$ 不可逆，负指数一般没有定义。

对不同矩阵，$(AB)^k=A^kB^k$ 一般不成立。取
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},$$
则 $AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$，故 $(AB)^2=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$；而
$$A^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad B^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
A^2B^2=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix},$$
两者不相等。若 $AB=BA$，则二项式定理成立：
$$(A+B)^m=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}A^iB^{m-i},$$
因为展开时的交叉项可以按 $A,B$ 的幂次合并；这可由归纳法证明。条件是 $AB=BA$，不能只因为 $A,B$ 都是方阵就套用。

若 $A$ 可对角化，即存在可逆 $P$ 与对角矩阵 $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ 使 $A=P\Lambda P^{-1}$，则对 $k\ge1$，
$$A^k=(P\Lambda P^{-1})^k=P\Lambda^kP^{-1}
=P\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n^k)P^{-1}.$$
证明用归纳：$k=1$ 时就是 $A$；若 $A^k=P\Lambda^kP^{-1}$，则
$$A^{k+1}=P\Lambda^kP^{-1}P\Lambda P^{-1}=P\Lambda^{k+1}P^{-1},$$
中间的 $P^{-1}P$ 抵消。前提是 $A$ 有 $n$ 个线性无关的特征向量；不可对角化时这条路线失效，应改用 Jordan 标准形或凯莱–哈密顿定理。

对多项式 $f(x)=a_mx^m+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$，定义**方阵多项式**
$$f(A)=a_mA^m+\cdots+a_1A+a_0E_n.$$
常数项必须写成 $a_0E_n$，因为矩阵只能与同阶矩阵相加。对同一个 $A$，任意两个多项式可交换：
$$f(A)g(A)=g(A)f(A),$$
因为每一项都是 $A$ 的幂的线性组合，而 $A^iA^j=A^{i+j}=A^jA^i$。若 $A\alpha=\lambda\alpha$ 且 $\alpha\ne0$，则 $A^i\alpha=\lambda^i\alpha$，从而
$$f(A)\alpha=f(\lambda)\alpha,$$
即 $f(\lambda)$ 是 $f(A)$ 的特征值；特别地，$A^k$ 的特征值是 $\lambda^k$。设 $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ 是 $A$ 的全部特征值（在 $\mathbb C$ 上按代数重数计），则 $f(A)$ 的全部特征值恰为 $f(\lambda_1),\dots,f(\lambda_n)$。

设特征多项式为
$$f(\lambda)=|\lambda E-A|=\lambda^n+c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda+c_0.$$
**凯莱–哈密顿定理**断言
$$f(A)=O,$$
对任意 $n$ 阶方阵成立，不要求可对角化。于是
$$A^n=-(c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A+c_0E),$$
任何 $A^k$（$k\ge n$）都可递推降为次数小于 $n$ 的多项式。又 $c_0=(-1)^n|A|$；若 $A$ 可逆，则 $c_0\ne0$，从 $f(A)=O$ 可解出
$$A^{-1}=-\frac{1}{c_0}\left(A^{n-1}+c_{n-1}A^{n-2}+\cdots+c_1E\right).$$
所以可逆矩阵的逆是 $A$ 的多项式。注意定理只给出 $f(A)=O$，不能反过来由某个 $f(A)=O$ 断定 $f$ 就是特征多项式——最小多项式可能次数更低。

例：$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$。令 $N=A-E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$，则 $N^2=O$，$A=E+N$，且 $E$ 与 $N$ 可交换，故二项式展开只剩前两项：
$$A^n=(E+N)^n=E+nN=\begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
验证：$n=1$ 给出 $A$；$n=2$ 给出 $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=A^2$。另一方面，特征多项式为 $f(\lambda)=(\lambda-1)^2$，凯莱–哈密顿给出 $(A-E)^2=N^2=O$，与直接计算一致。这个例子也说明 $A$ 不可对角化（两个特征值都是 $1$ 但 $A\ne E$），凯莱–哈密顿定理仍然适用。
en:
Let $A\in M_n(K)$. Define $A^1=A$ and $A^{k+1}=A^kA$, with the convention
$$A^0=E_n.$$
Here $A^0$ is the identity matrix, not the scalar $0$ or $1$. For a fixed $A$, the index laws
$$A^kA^l=A^{k+l},\qquad (A^k)^l=A^{kl}$$
follow by induction on $l$: $A^kA^{l+1}=A^kA^lA=A^{k+l}A=A^{k+l+1}$, and $(A^k)^{l+1}=(A^k)^lA^k=A^{kl}A^k=A^{k(l+1)}$. The proof uses only that powers of the same matrix commute. If $A$ is not invertible, negative exponents are generally undefined.

For different matrices, $(AB)^k=A^kB^k$ generally fails. Take
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $(AB)^2=\begin{pmatrix}5&3\\3&2\end{pmatrix}$, while
$$A^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad B^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
A^2B^2=\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix},$$
and the two results differ. If $AB=BA$, then the binomial theorem holds:
$$(A+B)^m=\sum_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}A^iB^{m-i},$$
because the cross terms can be combined by powers of $A$ and $B$; this follows by induction. The hypothesis is $AB=BA$; it is not enough that $A$ and $B$ are square.

If $A$ is diagonalizable, that is, $A=P\Lambda P^{-1}$ for some invertible $P$ and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, then for $k\ge1$,
$$A^k=(P\Lambda P^{-1})^k=P\Lambda^kP^{-1}
=P\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^k,\dots,\lambda_n^k)P^{-1}.$$
Induction proves it: for $k=1$ this is just $A$; if $A^k=P\Lambda^kP^{-1}$, then
$$A^{k+1}=P\Lambda^kP^{-1}P\Lambda P^{-1}=P\Lambda^{k+1}P^{-1},$$
with $P^{-1}P$ cancelling. The hypothesis is that $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors; if $A$ is not diagonalizable this route fails, and one should use the Jordan form or the Cayley–Hamilton theorem instead.

For a polynomial $f(x)=a_mx^m+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$, define the **matrix polynomial**
$$f(A)=a_mA^m+\cdots+a_1A+a_0E_n.$$
The constant term must be written $a_0E_n$, because a matrix can only be added to a matrix of the same size. For the same $A$, any two polynomials commute:
$$f(A)g(A)=g(A)f(A),$$
since each is a linear combination of powers of $A$ and $A^iA^j=A^{i+j}=A^jA^i$. If $A\alpha=\lambda\alpha$ with $\alpha\ne0$, then $A^i\alpha=\lambda^i\alpha$, hence
$$f(A)\alpha=f(\lambda)\alpha,$$
so $f(\lambda)$ is an eigenvalue of $f(A)$; in particular, the eigenvalues of $A^k$ are $\lambda^k$. Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ be all eigenvalues of $A$ (over $\mathbb C$, counted with algebraic multiplicity); then the eigenvalues of $f(A)$ are exactly $f(\lambda_1),\dots,f(\lambda_n)$.

Let the characteristic polynomial be
$$f(\lambda)=|\lambda E-A|=\lambda^n+c_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1\lambda+c_0.$$
The **Cayley–Hamilton theorem** states that
$$f(A)=O$$
for every $n\times n$ matrix, with no diagonalizability assumption. Hence
$$A^n=-(c_{n-1}A^{n-1}+\cdots+c_1A+c_0E),$$
and every $A^k$ with $k\ge n$ can be reduced recursively to a polynomial of degree less than $n$. Also $c_0=(-1)^n|A|$. If $A$ is invertible, then $c_0\ne0$, and $f(A)=O$ gives
$$A^{-1}=-\frac{1}{c_0}\left(A^{n-1}+c_{n-1}A^{n-2}+\cdots+c_1E\right).$$
Thus the inverse of an invertible matrix is a polynomial in $A$. Note that the theorem only asserts $f(A)=O$; conversely, $f(A)=O$ for some $f$ does not imply that $f$ is the characteristic polynomial, since the minimal polynomial may have lower degree.

Example: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Put $N=A-E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then $N^2=O$, $A=E+N$, and $E$ commutes with $N$, so the binomial expansion terminates after two terms:
$$A^n=(E+N)^n=E+nN=\begin{pmatrix}1&n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Check: $n=1$ gives $A$; $n=2$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}=A^2$. On the other hand, the characteristic polynomial is $f(\lambda)=(\lambda-1)^2$, and Cayley–Hamilton gives $(A-E)^2=N^2=O$, consistent with the direct computation. This example also shows that $A$ is not diagonalizable (both eigenvalues are $1$ but $A\ne E$), yet Cayley–Hamilton still applies.

设 $A=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ 为 $m\times n$ 实矩阵，且列向量线性无关（因此 $n\le m$）。Gram–Schmidt 正交化递推为
$$q_1=\frac{a_1}{\|a_1\|},\qquad
q_j=\frac{a_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i}
{\left\|a_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i\right\|}\quad(2\le j\le n).$$
列线性无关保证每一步的分子非零，故分母为正。移项得
$$a_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i+r_{jj}q_j,\qquad
r_{jj}=\left\|a_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i\right\|>0.$$
令 $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$，令 $r_{ij}=\langle a_j,q_i\rangle$（$i<j$），$r_{jj}$ 如上，$i>j$ 时 $r_{ij}=0$，则 $Q^{\mathrm T}Q=E_n$，$R=(r_{ij})$ 为上三角且对角元为正，并且
$$A=QR.$$
这就是 QR 分解的存在性构造。

形状方面：$Q$ 是 $m\times n$，$R$ 是 $n\times n$。条件 $Q^{\mathrm T}Q=E_n$ 只说明 $Q$ 的列正交标准；当 $m>n$ 时 $Q$ 不是方阵，$QQ^{\mathrm T}\ne E_m$，不要把它误当成正交矩阵。唯一性：若 $A=QR=Q'R'$，且两组都满足上述条件，则
$$Q=Q'T,\qquad T=R'R^{-1}.$$
$T$ 是上三角矩阵，且对角元为正（正数之积仍为正）。由 $Q,Q'$ 的列正交标准，
$$E_n=Q^{\mathrm T}Q=T^{\mathrm T}Q'^{\mathrm T}Q'T=T^{\mathrm T}T,$$
故 $T$ 是正交矩阵。上三角的正交矩阵只能是对角元为 $\pm1$ 的对角矩阵；而 $T$ 的对角元为正，所以 $T=E_n$。于是 $Q=Q'$、$R=R'$。这说明在“$R$ 对角元为正”的约定下 QR 分解唯一；若允许对角元取负，可逐列变号得到不同的分解。

设 $A$ 为任意 $m\times n$ 实矩阵。$A^{\mathrm T}A$ 是对称半正定矩阵：$(A^{\mathrm T}A)^{\mathrm T}=A^{\mathrm T}A$，且
$$x^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}Ax=\|Ax\|^2\ge0.$$
由实对称矩阵正交对角化，存在正交矩阵 $V=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ 使
$$A^{\mathrm T}AV=V\Lambda,\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n),$$
其中 $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0$。令 $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$，设非零奇异值的个数为 $r$。对 $i\le r$ 定义
$$u_i=\frac{Av_i}{\sigma_i}.$$
则
$$u_i^{\mathrm T}u_j=\frac{v_i^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}Av_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}
=\frac{\lambda_j\delta_{ij}}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}=\delta_{ij},$$
故 $u_1,\dots,u_r$ 是标准正交组；把它扩充为 $\mathbb R^m$ 的标准正交基 $u_1,\dots,u_m$。令 $U=(u_1,\dots,u_m)$，令 $\Sigma$ 为 $m\times n$ 矩阵，其前 $r$ 个对角元为 $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$，其余为 $0$。对 $i\le r$ 有 $Av_i=\sigma_i u_i$；对 $i>r$ 有 $\|Av_i\|^2=\lambda_i=0$，故 $Av_i=0$，而 $\Sigma$ 的第 $i$ 列也为零。于是 $AV=U\Sigma$，即
$$A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm T}.$$
若 $r=0$，则 $A=O$，取任意正交 $U,V$ 即可。

由 $A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm T}$ 且 $U,V$ 正交，$\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}\Sigma$，即秩等于非零奇异值的个数 $r$。又
$$A^{\mathrm T}A=V\Sigma^{\mathrm T}\Sigma V^{\mathrm T},$$
故 $A^{\mathrm T}A$ 的特征值为 $\sigma_i^2$（含零），奇异值按降序由 $A$ 唯一确定；$U,V$ 一般不唯一，因为相等奇异值对应的子空间或零奇异值对应的向量可以旋转。只保留非零项得到**紧（经济）型 SVD**：
$$A=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathrm T}.$$
范数方面，正交变换不改变谱范数与 Frobenius 范数，而 $\Sigma$ 的谱范数为 $\sigma_1$、Frobenius 范数平方为 $\sum_i\sigma_i^2$，所以
$$\|A\|_2=\sigma_1,\qquad \|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i^2.$$
$A$ 与 $A^{\mathrm T}$ 有相同的奇异值，$A^{\mathrm T}A$ 与 $AA^{\mathrm T}$ 的非零特征值都等于 $\sigma_i^2$。

设 $A$ 列满秩，$A=QR$。最小二乘问题 $\min_x\|Ax-b\|$ 中，把 $b$ 分解为 $b=QQ^{\mathrm T}b+(E_m-QQ^{\mathrm T})b$，并用 $Q^{\mathrm T}Q=E_n$，得
$$\|Ax-b\|^2=\|QRx-b\|^2
=\|Rx-Q^{\mathrm T}b\|^2+\|(E_m-QQ^{\mathrm T})b\|^2.$$
最后一项与 $x$ 无关，因为 $Q^{\mathrm T}(E_m-QQ^{\mathrm T})=0$。因此极小化等价于解上三角方程组
$$R\hat x=Q^{\mathrm T}b.$$
$R$ 的对角元为正，故 $R$ 可逆，回代得到唯一解 $\hat x=R^{-1}Q^{\mathrm T}b$。这里 $QQ^{\mathrm T}$ 是到 $\operatorname{col}(Q)=\operatorname{col}(A)$ 的正交投影；当 $m=n$ 时它就是 $E_m$，残差项消失。与正规方程 $A^{\mathrm T}Ax=A^{\mathrm T}b$ 相比，QR 方法不需构造 $A^{\mathrm T}A$，数值上更稳定。

设 $A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm T}$，$\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$，并设 $k<r$。截断 SVD 为
$$A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathrm T}.$$
Eckart–Young 定理断言：对任意秩不超过 $k$ 的 $m\times n$ 矩阵 $B$，
$$\|A-B\|_2\ge\sigma_{k+1},\qquad
\|A-B\|_F\ge\sqrt{\sum_{i=k+1}^{r}\sigma_i^2},$$
而 $B=A_k$ 同时达到这两个下界。谱范数下界的证明：若 $\operatorname{rank}B\le k$，则 $\dim\ker B\ge n-k$；子空间 $\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}\}$ 的维数为 $k+1$，故它与 $\ker B$ 有非零交向量 $z=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}c_iv_i$。于是
$$\|(A-B)z\|=\|Az\|=\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\sigma_i c_i u_i\right\|
\ge\sigma_{k+1}\|z\|,$$
故 $\|A-B\|_2\ge\sigma_{k+1}$。Frobenius 下界可由奇异值的 Hoffman–Wielandt 不等式得到；而 $A-A_k=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i u_iv_i^{\mathrm T}$，这些秩一矩阵在 Frobenius 内积下两两正交，故其谱范数为 $\sigma_{k+1}$、Frobenius 范数为 $\sqrt{\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2}$。所以 $A_k$ 是谱范数与 Frobenius 范数下的最佳秩 $k$ 逼近；最佳矩阵不一定唯一。
en:
Let $A=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$ be a real $m\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent (hence $n\le m$). The Gram–Schmidt recursion is
$$q_1=\frac{a_1}{\|a_1\|},\qquad
q_j=\frac{a_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i}
{\left\|a_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i\right\|}\quad(2\le j\le n).$$
Linear independence of the columns guarantees that each numerator is nonzero, so every denominator is positive. Rearranging gives
$$a_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i+r_{jj}q_j,\qquad
r_{jj}=\left\|a_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}\langle a_j,q_i\rangle q_i\right\|>0.$$
Let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$; let $r_{ij}=\langle a_j,q_i\rangle$ for $i<j$, let $r_{jj}$ be as above, and set $r_{ij}=0$ for $i>j$. Then $Q^{\mathrm T}Q=E_n$, $R=(r_{ij})$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal, and
$$A=QR.$$
This constructs the QR factorization and proves existence.

Shapes: $Q$ is $m\times n$ and $R$ is $n\times n$. The condition $Q^{\mathrm T}Q=E_n$ says only that the columns of $Q$ are orthonormal; when $m>n$, $Q$ is not square and $QQ^{\mathrm T}\ne E_m$, so it must not be treated as an orthogonal matrix. Uniqueness: if $A=QR=Q'R'$ and both pairs satisfy the stated conditions, then
$$Q=Q'T,\qquad T=R'R^{-1}.$$
$T$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal (a product of positive numbers is positive). Since $Q$ and $Q'$ have orthonormal columns,
$$E_n=Q^{\mathrm T}Q=T^{\mathrm T}Q'^{\mathrm T}Q'T=T^{\mathrm T}T,$$
so $T$ is orthogonal. An upper triangular orthogonal matrix must be diagonal with entries $\pm1$; since the diagonal of $T$ is positive, $T=E_n$. Hence $Q=Q'$ and $R=R'$. Thus QR is unique under the convention of positive diagonal entries in $R$; if negative diagonal entries are allowed, flipping signs column by column produces different factorizations.

Let $A$ be an arbitrary real $m\times n$ matrix. Then $A^{\mathrm T}A$ is symmetric positive semidefinite: $(A^{\mathrm T}A)^{\mathrm T}=A^{\mathrm T}A$ and
$$x^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}Ax=\|Ax\|^2\ge0.$$
By orthogonal diagonalization of real symmetric matrices, there is an orthogonal matrix $V=(v_1,\dots,v_n)$ such that
$$A^{\mathrm T}AV=V\Lambda,\qquad \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n),$$
with $\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n\ge0$. Put $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$ and let $r$ be the number of nonzero singular values. For $i\le r$ define
$$u_i=\frac{Av_i}{\sigma_i}.$$
Then
$$u_i^{\mathrm T}u_j=\frac{v_i^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}Av_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}
=\frac{\lambda_j\delta_{ij}}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}=\delta_{ij},$$
so $u_1,\dots,u_r$ is an orthonormal set; extend it to an orthonormal basis $u_1,\dots,u_m$ of $\mathbb R^m$. Let $U=(u_1,\dots,u_m)$, and let $\Sigma$ be the $m\times n$ matrix whose first $r$ diagonal entries are $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ and whose other entries are $0$. For $i\le r$, $Av_i=\sigma_i u_i$; for $i>r$, $\|Av_i\|^2=\lambda_i=0$, so $Av_i=0$, while the $i$-th column of $\Sigma$ is also zero. Therefore $AV=U\Sigma$, that is,
$$A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm T}.$$
If $r=0$, then $A=O$ and any orthogonal $U,V$ work.

Since $A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm T}$ with $U,V$ orthogonal, $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}\Sigma$, so the rank equals the number $r$ of nonzero singular values. Also
$$A^{\mathrm T}A=V\Sigma^{\mathrm T}\Sigma V^{\mathrm T},$$
so the eigenvalues of $A^{\mathrm T}A$ are $\sigma_i^2$ (including zeros), and the singular values are uniquely determined by $A$ in decreasing order. The matrices $U,V$ are generally not unique, since equal singular values or zero singular values allow rotations within the corresponding subspaces. Keeping only nonzero terms gives the **compact (economy) SVD**
$$A=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathrm T}.$$
As for norms, orthogonal transformations preserve both the spectral and Frobenius norms, while $\Sigma$ has spectral norm $\sigma_1$ and squared Frobenius norm $\sum_i\sigma_i^2$; hence
$$\|A\|_2=\sigma_1,\qquad \|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i^2.$$
$A$ and $A^{\mathrm T}$ have the same singular values, and $A^{\mathrm T}A$ and $AA^{\mathrm T}$ have the same nonzero eigenvalues, all equal to $\sigma_i^2$.

Let $A$ have full column rank and $A=QR$. In the least-squares problem $\min_x\|Ax-b\|$, decompose $b=QQ^{\mathrm T}b+(E_m-QQ^{\mathrm T})b$ and use $Q^{\mathrm T}Q=E_n$ to get
$$\|Ax-b\|^2=\|QRx-b\|^2
=\|Rx-Q^{\mathrm T}b\|^2+\|(E_m-QQ^{\mathrm T})b\|^2.$$
The last term is independent of $x$, because $Q^{\mathrm T}(E_m-QQ^{\mathrm T})=0$. Hence minimizing is equivalent to solving the upper triangular system
$$R\hat x=Q^{\mathrm T}b.$$
The diagonal of $R$ is positive, so $R$ is invertible and back substitution gives the unique solution $\hat x=R^{-1}Q^{\mathrm T}b$. Here $QQ^{\mathrm T}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{col}(Q)=\operatorname{col}(A)$; when $m=n$ it equals $E_m$ and the residual term disappears. Compared with the normal equations $A^{\mathrm T}Ax=A^{\mathrm T}b$, the QR approach avoids forming $A^{\mathrm T}A$ and is numerically more stable.

Let $A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm T}$ with $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$, and let $k<r$. The truncated SVD is
$$A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathrm T}.$$
The Eckart–Young theorem states that for every $m\times n$ matrix $B$ of rank at most $k$,
$$\|A-B\|_2\ge\sigma_{k+1},\qquad
\|A-B\|_F\ge\sqrt{\sum_{i=k+1}^{r}\sigma_i^2},$$
and $B=A_k$ attains both bounds. For the spectral bound: if $\operatorname{rank}B\le k$, then $\dim\ker B\ge n-k$; the subspace $\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_{k+1}\}$ has dimension $k+1$, so it contains a nonzero vector $z=\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}c_iv_i$ lying in $\ker B$. Then
$$\|(A-B)z\|=\|Az\|=\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\sigma_i c_i u_i\right\|
\ge\sigma_{k+1}\|z\|,$$
so $\|A-B\|_2\ge\sigma_{k+1}$. The Frobenius bound follows from the Hoffman–Wielandt inequality for singular values. On the other hand, $A-A_k=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i u_iv_i^{\mathrm T}$; these rank-one terms are mutually orthogonal in the Frobenius inner product, so the spectral norm is $\sigma_{k+1}$ and the squared Frobenius norm is $\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$. Thus $A_k$ is a best rank-$k$ approximation in both the spectral and Frobenius norms; the best matrix need not be unique.

zh: 设 $A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$。若 $X\in\mathbb C^{n\times m}$ 满足四条 **Penrose 方程** $$\begin{aligned}&(1)\ AXA=A,\\&(2)\ XAX=X,\\&(3)\ (AX)^{\mathrm H}=AX,\\&(4)\ (XA)^{\mathrm H}=XA,\end{aligned}$$ 则称 $X=A^{+}$ 为 $A$ 的 **Moore–Penrose 广义逆**。形状必须匹配：$A$ 是 $m\times n$，$A^{+}$ 必须是 $n\times m$，这样 $AX$ 为 $m$ 阶、$XA$ 为 $n$ 阶，Hermitian 条件才有意义。对任意矩阵（奇异、矩形、零矩阵）四条方程的解存在且唯一。当 $A$ 可逆时，仅 $(1)(2)$ 就迫使 $X=A^{-1}$；广义逆多出两条 Hermitian 条件，正是为了在秩亏或矩形情形下仍然锁定唯一解。

唯一性证明。设 $X,Y$ 都满足四条方程。先证 $AX=AY$：由 $(1)(2)$，
$$(AX)^2=AXAX=A(XAX)=AX,$$
且 $(AX)^{\mathrm H}=AX$，故 $AX$ 是 Hermitian 幂等阵；它的像含于 $\operatorname{col}(A)$，而在 $\operatorname{col}(A)$ 上恒等（对 $v=Au$，$AXv=AXAu=Au=v$），所以 $AX$ 是到 $\operatorname{col}(A)$ 的正交投影。同理 $AY$ 也是到同一子空间的正交投影，而正交投影由子空间唯一确定，故 $AX=AY$。
再证 $XA=YA$：$XA$ 是 Hermitian 幂等阵，且 $\operatorname{col}(XA)=\operatorname{col}(X)$（由 $X=XAX$）。又
$$X=(XA)^{\mathrm H}X=A^{\mathrm H}X^{\mathrm H}X,$$
故 $\operatorname{col}(X)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$；而 $A=AXA$ 与 $X=XAX$ 给出 $\operatorname{rank}A\le\operatorname{rank}X\le\operatorname{rank}A$，所以 $\operatorname{rank}X=\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}A^{\mathrm H}$，从而 $\operatorname{col}(X)=\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$。同理 $\operatorname{col}(Y)=\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$，故 $XA=YA$。
最后
$$X=XAX=X(AX)=X(AY)=(XA)Y=(YA)Y=YAY=Y,$$
唯一性得证。

存在性用 SVD 构造。设
$$A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}$$
为满型 SVD：$U$ 为 $m$ 阶酉矩阵，$V$ 为 $n$ 阶酉矩阵，$\Sigma$ 为 $m\times n$，对角元 $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$，其余为 $0$。定义 $\Sigma^{+}$ 为 $n\times m$ 矩阵：把 $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ 换成 $1/\sigma_1,\dots,1/\sigma_r$ 并放在转置位置，其余为 $0$。令
$$X=V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H}.$$
直接代入，利用 $V^{\mathrm H}V=I$、$U^{\mathrm H}U=I$ 与 $\Sigma\Sigma^{+}\Sigma=\Sigma$：
$$AXA=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H}U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}
=U\Sigma\Sigma^{+}\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}=A.$$
同理 $XAX=X$，因为 $\Sigma^{+}\Sigma\Sigma^{+}=\Sigma^{+}$。又
$$AX=U\Sigma\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H},\qquad XA=V\Sigma^{+}\Sigma V^{\mathrm H},$$
而 $\Sigma\Sigma^{+}$ 与 $\Sigma^{+}\Sigma$ 都是对角元为 $1$（前 $r$ 个）和 $0$ 的 Hermitian 幂等阵，故 $(AX)^{\mathrm H}=AX$、$(XA)^{\mathrm H}=XA$。于是 $X$ 满足四条方程，由唯一性 $A^{+}=V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H}$。

满秩情形的显式公式。若 $A$ 列满秩（$r=n\le m$），则 $A^{\mathrm H}A$ 可逆：若 $A^{\mathrm H}Ax=0$，则
$$0=x^{\mathrm H}A^{\mathrm H}Ax=\|Ax\|^2,$$
故 $Ax=0$，再由列满秩得 $x=0$。令
$$X=(A^{\mathrm H}A)^{-1}A^{\mathrm H}.$$
则 $XA=E_n$，于是 $XAX=X$、$AXA=A$ 自动成立；$XA=E_n$ 是 Hermitian，且
$$AX=A(A^{\mathrm H}A)^{-1}A^{\mathrm H}$$
是 Hermitian 幂等阵（到 $\operatorname{col}(A)$ 的正交投影）。所以
$$A^{+}=(A^{\mathrm H}A)^{-1}A^{\mathrm H},$$
这是 $A$ 的**左逆**。若 $A$ 行满秩（$r=m\le n$），同理 $AA^{\mathrm H}$ 可逆，且
$$A^{+}=A^{\mathrm H}(AA^{\mathrm H})^{-1},\qquad AA^{+}=E_m,$$
这是**右逆**。两个条件不能互换：列满秩用 $A^{\mathrm H}A$，行满秩用 $AA^{\mathrm H}$。若 $A$ 可逆，两式都化为 $A^{-1}$。

最小二乘最小范数解。对任意 $b$，令 $x^{+}=A^{+}b$。把 $b$ 分解为
$$b_1=AA^{+}b\in\operatorname{col}(A),\qquad
b_2=(E_m-AA^{+})b\in\operatorname{col}(A)^{\perp},$$
因为 $AA^{+}$ 是到 $\operatorname{col}(A)$ 的正交投影。对任意 $x$，$Ax\in\operatorname{col}(A)$，故
$$\|Ax-b\|^2=\|Ax-b_1\|^2+\|b_2\|^2\ge\|b_2\|^2,$$
等号当且仅当 $Ax=b_1$。而 $Ax^{+}=AA^{+}b=b_1$，所以 $x^{+}$ 是最小二乘解。若 $x$ 也是最小二乘解，则 $Ax=Ax^{+}$，即 $x-x^{+}\in\ker A$。又 $x^{+}=A^{+}b\in\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$，而
$$\ker A=(\operatorname{col}A^{\mathrm H})^{\perp},$$
故由勾股定理
$$\|x\|^2=\|x^{+}\|^2+\|x-x^{+}\|^2\ge\|x^{+}\|^2,$$
等号仅当 $x=x^{+}$。因此 $x^{+}$ 是唯一的最小范数最小二乘解；全部最小二乘解为
$$x^{+}+(E_n-A^{+}A)y,\qquad y\in\mathbb C^n\ \text{任意}.$$

无条件恒等式与反序律。由 $A=AA^{+}A$ 与 $A^{+}=A^{+}AA^{+}$ 夹逼得 $$\operatorname{rank}A^{+}=\operatorname{rank}A.$$ 四条方程在把 $A$ 与 $A^{+}$ 互换后仍然成立，故 $$(A^{+})^{+}=A.$$ 对四条方程整体取 Hermitian 转置，可知 $(A^{\mathrm H})^{+}=(A^{+})^{\mathrm H}$。但反序律一般失败：$$(AB)^{+}\ne B^{+}A^{+}.$$ 例如 $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}$、$B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$，则 $AB=(1)$ 可逆，$(AB)^{+}=(1)$；而 $$A^{+}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B^{+}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B^{+}A^{+}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=\frac12\ne(1).$$ 反序律成立的常用充分条件是 $A$ 列满秩且 $B$ 行满秩（此时 $A^{+}A=E$、$BB^{+}=E$），但不能把它当成普遍公式。
en: Let $A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$. If $X\in\mathbb C^{n\times m}$ satisfies the four **Penrose equations** $$\begin{aligned}&(1)\ AXA=A,\\&(2)\ XAX=X,\\&(3)\ (AX)^{\mathrm H}=AX,\\&(4)\ (XA)^{\mathrm H}=XA,\end{aligned}$$ then $X=A^{+}$ is the **Moore–Penrose inverse** of $A$. The shapes must match: $A$ is $m\times n$, so $A^{+}$ must be $n\times m$; then $AX$ is $m\times m$ and $XA$ is $n\times n$, which makes the Hermitian conditions meaningful. For every matrix — singular, rectangular, or zero — a solution of the four equations exists and is unique. When $A$ is invertible, $(1)(2)$ alone force $X=A^{-1}$; the two extra Hermitian conditions are exactly what pins down a unique generalized inverse in the rank-deficient or rectangular case.

Proof of uniqueness. Suppose $X$ and $Y$ both satisfy the four equations. First show $AX=AY$. From $(1)(2)$,
$$(AX)^2=AXAX=A(XAX)=AX,$$
and $(AX)^{\mathrm H}=AX$, so $AX$ is Hermitian and idempotent. Its range lies in $\operatorname{col}(A)$, and it fixes $\operatorname{col}(A)$: for $v=Au$, $AXv=AXAu=Au=v$. Hence $AX$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{col}(A)$. Likewise $AY$ is the orthogonal projection onto the same subspace, and an orthogonal projection is determined by its subspace, so $AX=AY$.
Next show $XA=YA$. The matrix $XA$ is Hermitian and idempotent, and $\operatorname{col}(XA)=\operatorname{col}(X)$ because $X=XAX$. Moreover
$$X=(XA)^{\mathrm H}X=A^{\mathrm H}X^{\mathrm H}X,$$
so $\operatorname{col}(X)\subseteq\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$. From $A=AXA$ and $X=XAX$ we get $\operatorname{rank}A\le\operatorname{rank}X\le\operatorname{rank}A$, hence $\operatorname{rank}X=\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}A^{\mathrm H}$, and therefore $\operatorname{col}(X)=\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$. The same argument gives $\operatorname{col}(Y)=\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$, so $XA=YA$.
Finally,
$$X=XAX=X(AX)=X(AY)=(XA)Y=(YA)Y=YAY=Y,$$
which proves uniqueness.

Existence is constructed from the SVD. Let
$$A=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}$$
be a full SVD: $U$ is unitary of order $m$, $V$ is unitary of order $n$, and $\Sigma$ is $m\times n$ with diagonal entries $\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ and zeros elsewhere. Define $\Sigma^{+}$ as the $n\times m$ matrix obtained by replacing $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_r$ by $1/\sigma_1,\dots,1/\sigma_r$ in the transposed positions and setting all other entries to $0$. Put
$$X=V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H}.$$
Using $V^{\mathrm H}V=I$, $U^{\mathrm H}U=I$, and $\Sigma\Sigma^{+}\Sigma=\Sigma$,
$$AXA=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H}U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}
=U\Sigma\Sigma^{+}\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}=U\Sigma V^{\mathrm H}=A.$$
Similarly $XAX=X$, because $\Sigma^{+}\Sigma\Sigma^{+}=\Sigma^{+}$. Also
$$AX=U\Sigma\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H},\qquad XA=V\Sigma^{+}\Sigma V^{\mathrm H},$$
and $\Sigma\Sigma^{+}$ and $\Sigma^{+}\Sigma$ are Hermitian idempotent matrices with $r$ ones and the remaining diagonal entries zero. Hence $(AX)^{\mathrm H}=AX$ and $(XA)^{\mathrm H}=XA$. Thus $X$ satisfies all four equations, and uniqueness gives $A^{+}=V\Sigma^{+}U^{\mathrm H}$.

Explicit formulas in the full-rank cases. If $A$ has full column rank ($r=n\le m$), then $A^{\mathrm H}A$ is invertible: if $A^{\mathrm H}Ax=0$, then
$$0=x^{\mathrm H}A^{\mathrm H}Ax=\|Ax\|^2,$$
so $Ax=0$, and full column rank forces $x=0$. Set
$$X=(A^{\mathrm H}A)^{-1}A^{\mathrm H}.$$
Then $XA=E_n$, so $XAX=X$ and $AXA=A$ hold automatically. Moreover $XA=E_n$ is Hermitian, and
$$AX=A(A^{\mathrm H}A)^{-1}A^{\mathrm H}$$
is Hermitian and idempotent (the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{col}(A)$). Therefore
$$A^{+}=(A^{\mathrm H}A)^{-1}A^{\mathrm H},$$
the **left inverse** of $A$. If $A$ has full row rank ($r=m\le n$), then $AA^{\mathrm H}$ is invertible and, analogously,
$$A^{+}=A^{\mathrm H}(AA^{\mathrm H})^{-1},\qquad AA^{+}=E_m,$$
the **right inverse**. The hypotheses must not be interchanged: full column rank uses $A^{\mathrm H}A$, full row rank uses $AA^{\mathrm H}$. If $A$ is invertible, both formulas reduce to $A^{-1}$.

Least-squares minimum-norm solution. For any $b$, let $x^{+}=A^{+}b$. Decompose $b$ as
$$b_1=AA^{+}b\in\operatorname{col}(A),\qquad
b_2=(E_m-AA^{+})b\in\operatorname{col}(A)^{\perp},$$
since $AA^{+}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\operatorname{col}(A)$. For every $x$, $Ax\in\operatorname{col}(A)$, so
$$\|Ax-b\|^2=\|Ax-b_1\|^2+\|b_2\|^2\ge\|b_2\|^2,$$
with equality exactly when $Ax=b_1$. Since $Ax^{+}=AA^{+}b=b_1$, the vector $x^{+}$ is a least-squares solution. If $x$ is also a least-squares solution, then $Ax=Ax^{+}$, so $x-x^{+}\in\ker A$. Also $x^{+}=A^{+}b\in\operatorname{col}(A^{\mathrm H})$, and
$$\ker A=(\operatorname{col}A^{\mathrm H})^{\perp}.$$
By Pythagoras,
$$\|x\|^2=\|x^{+}\|^2+\|x-x^{+}\|^2\ge\|x^{+}\|^2,$$
with equality only when $x=x^{+}$. Hence $x^{+}$ is the unique least-squares solution of minimum norm; all least-squares solutions are
$$x^{+}+(E_n-A^{+}A)y,\qquad y\in\mathbb C^n\ \text{arbitrary}.$$

Unconditional identities and the reverse-order law. From $A=AA^{+}A$ and $A^{+}=A^{+}AA^{+}$, $$\operatorname{rank}A^{+}=\operatorname{rank}A.$$ The four equations remain valid after interchanging $A$ and $A^{+}$, so $$(A^{+})^{+}=A.$$ Taking the Hermitian transpose of all four equations gives $(A^{\mathrm H})^{+}=(A^{+})^{\mathrm H}$. The reverse-order law, however, fails in general: $$(AB)^{+}\ne B^{+}A^{+}.$$ For example, take $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. Then $AB=(1)$ is invertible and $(AB)^{+}=(1)$, while $$A^{+}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B^{+}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad B^{+}A^{+}=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=\frac12\ne(1).$$ A common sufficient condition for the reverse-order law is that $A$ have full column rank and $B$ full row rank (then $A^{+}A=E$ and $BB^{+}=E$), but it is not a universal formula.

zh:
设 $K=\mathbb R$ 或 $\mathbb C$，$M_n(K)$ 为 $n$ 阶方阵。子集 $G\subseteq M_n(K)$ 称为**矩阵群**，若：$E_n\in G$；$A,B\in G\Rightarrow AB\in G$；$A\in G\Rightarrow A$ 可逆且 $A^{-1}\in G$。等价地，$G$ 在矩阵乘法下构成群。最基本的例子是
$$GL(n,K)=\{A\in M_n(K):\det A\ne0\},$$
称为**一般线性群**。它确实是群：$\det(AB)=\det A\det B\ne0$，$\det E=1$，且 $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det A$，所以乘法封闭、单位元在、逆元在；结合律由矩阵乘法自动继承。$GL(n,K)$ 的元素正是 $K^n$ 上可逆线性变换在标准基下的矩阵。

行列式给出群同态
$$\det:GL(n,K)\to K^{\times},$$
其中 $K^{\times}=K\setminus\{0\}$ 在乘法下是群；$\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ 说明它是同态。其核
$$SL(n,K)=\{A\in GL(n,K):\det A=1\}$$
称为**特殊线性群**。核自动是正规子群：若 $S\in SL(n,K)$、$P\in GL(n,K)$，则
$$\det(P^{-1}SP)=\det(P)^{-1}\det(S)\det(P)=1,$$
故 $P^{-1}SP\in SL(n,K)$。几何上，$SL(n,\mathbb R)$ 由保持有向体积的线性变换组成；当 $n\ge2$ 时它不是 $O(n)$ 的子群，两者只在
$$SL(n,\mathbb R)\cap O(n)=SO(n)$$
处相交。

**正交群**
$$O(n)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb R):A^{\mathrm T}A=E_n\}.$$
若 $A,B\in O(n)$，则
$$(AB)^{\mathrm T}(AB)=B^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}AB=B^{\mathrm T}B=E_n,$$
故 $AB\in O(n)$；$E_n\in O(n)$；$A^{\mathrm T}A=E_n$ 说明 $A$ 可逆且 $A^{-1}=A^{\mathrm T}$，而 $A^{\mathrm T}\in O(n)$，故 $A^{-1}\in O(n)$。所以 $O(n)$ 是矩阵群。取行列式得
$$(\det A)^2=\det(A^{\mathrm T}A)=\det E_n=1,$$
故 $\det A=\pm1$。令
$$SO(n)=\{A\in O(n):\det A=1\}=O(n)\cap SL(n,\mathbb R),$$
它是 $O(n)$ 的指数 $2$ 子群（$n\ge1$）：$\det$ 在 $O(n)$ 上取到 $+1$ 与 $-1$（例如 $E_n$ 与 $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,\dots,1)$），两个陪集分别为 $SO(n)$ 与 $\{A\in O(n):\det A=-1\}$。

**酉群**
$$U(n)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):A^{\mathrm H}A=E_n\},\qquad A^{\mathrm H}=\overline{A}^{\mathrm T}.$$
与正交群同样的计算：若 $A,B\in U(n)$，则
$$(AB)^{\mathrm H}(AB)=B^{\mathrm H}A^{\mathrm H}AB=B^{\mathrm H}B=E_n,$$
且 $A^{-1}=A^{\mathrm H}\in U(n)$，故 $U(n)$ 是矩阵群。取行列式得
$$|\det A|^2=\det(A^{\mathrm H}A)=1,$$
即 $\det A$ 是模为 $1$ 的复数；注意这不是 $\det A=\pm1$，复数情形条件更弱。**特殊酉群**为
$$SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}=U(n)\cap SL(n,\mathbb C).$$
实正交矩阵是酉矩阵的特例：
$$O(n)=U(n)\cap M_n(\mathbb R).$$
$U(n)$ 的元素是 $\mathbb C^n$ 上保持 Hermitian 内积 $\langle x,y\rangle=y^{\mathrm H}x$ 的线性变换的矩阵。

对 $A\in O(n)$ 与 $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$，
$$\langle Ax,Ay\rangle=(Ax)^{\mathrm T}(Ay)=x^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}Ay=x^{\mathrm T}y=\langle x,y\rangle.$$
取 $y=x$ 得 $\|Ax\|=\|x\|$。反过来，若 $A$ 对所有 $x,y$ 都保内积，取标准基 $e_i,e_j$ 得
$$(A^{\mathrm T}A)_{ij}=\langle Ae_i,Ae_j\rangle=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij},$$
故 $A^{\mathrm T}A=E_n$。所以 $O(n)$ 恰好是保长度、保内积的矩阵群。二维情形可完全参数化：若 $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in SO(2)$，由 $A^{\mathrm T}A=E_2$ 与 $\det A=1$ 得 $A^{-1}=A^{\mathrm T}=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\b&d\end{pmatrix}$，而 $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$，比较得 $d=a$、$c=-b$、$a^2+b^2=1$，故存在唯一 $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ 使
$$A=R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.$$
并且 $R(\theta)R(\varphi)=R(\theta+\varphi)$、$R(0)=E_2$、$R(\theta)^{-1}=R(-\theta)$，所以 $SO(2)\cong U(1)$（映射 $R(\theta)\mapsto e^{i\theta}$）。$SO(3)$ 则不交换：两个不同轴的三维旋转一般不可交换。

固定 $P\in GL(n,K)$，**相似变换** $A\mapsto P^{-1}AP$ 与**合同变换** $A\mapsto P^{\mathrm T}AP$ 都是 $GL(n,K)$ 在矩阵空间上的作用，但作用对象与不变量不同。相似来自换基：若线性变换 $T$ 在基 $\mathcal B$ 下的矩阵为 $A$，在新基 $\mathcal B'$ 下为 $P^{-1}AP$，其中 $P$ 是过渡矩阵；因此相似保持特征多项式、特征值、迹、行列式、秩与 Jordan 标准形。合同来自二次型或双线性型的换基：若 $A$ 对称，则
$$(P^{\mathrm T}AP)^{\mathrm T}=P^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}P=P^{\mathrm T}AP,$$
仍对称；合同保持秩与惯性指数 $(p,q)$（Sylvester 惯性定理），但一般**不保持特征值**。例如
$$A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1),\qquad P=\operatorname{diag}(2,1),$$
则 $P^{\mathrm T}AP=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)$，特征值从 $(1,1)$ 变为 $(4,1)$，而秩与正惯性指数不变。复 Hermitian 情形把 $P^{\mathrm T}$ 换成 $P^{\mathrm H}$；相似与合同是两种不同的作用，不能混用不变量。

Let $K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let $M_n(K)$ be the set of $n\times n$ matrices. A subset $G\subseteq M_n(K)$ is a **matrix group** if $E_n\in G$; $A,B\in G$ implies $AB\in G$; and $A\in G$ implies $A$ is invertible with $A^{-1}\in G$. Equivalently, $G$ is a group under matrix multiplication. The basic example is
$$GL(n,K)=\{A\in M_n(K):\det A\ne0\},$$
the **general linear group**. It is indeed a group: $\det(AB)=\det A\det B\ne0$, $\det E=1$, and $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det A$, so it is closed under multiplication and contains the identity and inverses; associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication. The elements of $GL(n,K)$ are exactly the matrices of invertible linear transformations of $K^n$ in the standard basis.

The determinant gives a group homomorphism
$$\det:GL(n,K)\to K^{\times},$$
where $K^{\times}=K\setminus\{0\}$ is a group under multiplication; $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$ shows that it is a homomorphism. Its kernel
$$SL(n,K)=\{A\in GL(n,K):\det A=1\}$$
is the **special linear group**. A kernel is automatically normal: if $S\in SL(n,K)$ and $P\in GL(n,K)$, then
$$\det(P^{-1}SP)=\det(P)^{-1}\det(S)\det(P)=1,$$
so $P^{-1}SP\in SL(n,K)$. Geometrically, $SL(n,\mathbb R)$ consists of the linear transformations preserving oriented volume; for $n\ge2$ it is not a subgroup of $O(n)$, and the two meet exactly in
$$SL(n,\mathbb R)\cap O(n)=SO(n).$$

The **orthogonal group** is
$$O(n)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb R):A^{\mathrm T}A=E_n\}.$$
If $A,B\in O(n)$, then
$$(AB)^{\mathrm T}(AB)=B^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}AB=B^{\mathrm T}B=E_n,$$
so $AB\in O(n)$; $E_n\in O(n)$; and $A^{\mathrm T}A=E_n$ shows that $A$ is invertible with $A^{-1}=A^{\mathrm T}$, while $A^{\mathrm T}\in O(n)$, so $A^{-1}\in O(n)$. Hence $O(n)$ is a matrix group. Taking determinants,
$$(\det A)^2=\det(A^{\mathrm T}A)=\det E_n=1,$$
so $\det A=\pm1$. Define
$$SO(n)=\{A\in O(n):\det A=1\}=O(n)\cap SL(n,\mathbb R).$$
It has index $2$ in $O(n)$ for $n\ge1$: $\det$ takes both values $+1$ and $-1$ on $O(n)$ (for instance at $E_n$ and $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,\dots,1)$), and the two cosets are $SO(n)$ and $\{A\in O(n):\det A=-1\}$.

The **unitary group** is
$$U(n)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):A^{\mathrm H}A=E_n\},\qquad A^{\mathrm H}=\overline{A}^{\mathrm T}.$$
The computation is the same as for the orthogonal group: if $A,B\in U(n)$, then
$$(AB)^{\mathrm H}(AB)=B^{\mathrm H}A^{\mathrm H}AB=B^{\mathrm H}B=E_n,$$
and $A^{-1}=A^{\mathrm H}\in U(n)$, so $U(n)$ is a matrix group. Taking determinants,
$$|\det A|^2=\det(A^{\mathrm H}A)=1,$$
so $\det A$ is a complex number of modulus $1$; this is not the condition $\det A=\pm1$, which is stronger. The **special unitary group** is
$$SU(n)=\{A\in U(n):\det A=1\}=U(n)\cap SL(n,\mathbb C).$$
Real orthogonal matrices are special unitary ones:
$$O(n)=U(n)\cap M_n(\mathbb R).$$
Elements of $U(n)$ are the matrices of linear transformations of $\mathbb C^n$ preserving the Hermitian inner product $\langle x,y\rangle=y^{\mathrm H}x$.

For $A\in O(n)$ and $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$\langle Ax,Ay\rangle=(Ax)^{\mathrm T}(Ay)=x^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}Ay=x^{\mathrm T}y=\langle x,y\rangle.$$
Taking $y=x$ gives $\|Ax\|=\|x\|$. Conversely, if $A$ preserves all inner products, then taking $x=e_i$, $y=e_j$ in the standard basis gives
$$(A^{\mathrm T}A)_{ij}=\langle Ae_i,Ae_j\rangle=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij},$$
so $A^{\mathrm T}A=E_n$. Thus $O(n)$ is exactly the group of matrices preserving lengths and inner products. In dimension two there is a complete parametrization: if $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\in SO(2)$, then $A^{\mathrm T}A=E_2$ and $\det A=1$ give $A^{-1}=A^{\mathrm T}=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\b&d\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$; comparing them yields $d=a$, $c=-b$, and $a^2+b^2=1$, so there is a unique $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ with
$$A=R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}.$$
Moreover $R(\theta)R(\varphi)=R(\theta+\varphi)$, $R(0)=E_2$, and $R(\theta)^{-1}=R(-\theta)$, so $SO(2)\cong U(1)$ via $R(\theta)\mapsto e^{i\theta}$. By contrast, $SO(3)$ is not abelian: rotations about different axes generally do not commute.

Fix $P\in GL(n,K)$. The **similarity transformation** $A\mapsto P^{-1}AP$ and the **congruence transformation** $A\mapsto P^{\mathrm T}AP$ are both actions of $GL(n,K)$ on matrix space, but they act on different objects and preserve different invariants. Similarity comes from a change of basis: if a linear map $T$ has matrix $A$ in a basis $\mathcal B$ and matrix $P^{-1}AP$ in a new basis $\mathcal B'$, where $P$ is the transition matrix, then similarity preserves the characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, trace, determinant, rank, and Jordan form. Congruence comes from a change of basis for a quadratic or bilinear form: if $A$ is symmetric, then
$$(P^{\mathrm T}AP)^{\mathrm T}=P^{\mathrm T}A^{\mathrm T}P=P^{\mathrm T}AP,$$
so it remains symmetric. Congruence preserves rank and the inertia indices $(p,q)$ by Sylvester's law of inertia, but it generally **does not preserve eigenvalues**. For example,
$$A=\operatorname{diag}(1,1),\qquad P=\operatorname{diag}(2,1),$$
give $P^{\mathrm T}AP=\operatorname{diag}(4,1)$: the eigenvalues change from $(1,1)$ to $(4,1)$, while the rank and positive inertia index stay the same. For complex Hermitian forms, replace $P^{\mathrm T}$ by $P^{\mathrm H}$. Similarity and congruence are different actions, and their invariants must not be mixed.
